\runninghead{Readiness audits for dispute-key availability}

\title{KEYSTONE: Readiness Audits for Dispute-Key Availability in Encrypted Rollups}

\author{[Author details removed for peer review]}

\begin{abstract}
Encrypted optimistic rollups can keep ciphertexts and execution receipts available and still fail a dispute because the threshold service that must decrypt the disputed record is unavailable, late or uncooperative. We call the missing property dispute-key availability (DKA) and separate it from ciphertext availability, valid-share registration, audit-time readiness, authorized decryptability and deadline liveness. KEYSTONE audits readiness with sampled canary shares carrying Chaum--Pedersen proofs; their transcripts are simulatable from public shares, so audits exercise real shares without revealing any record. We give exact operating characteristics and show that a single small audit cannot separate a committee one share short of its threshold from a live one, whereas sequential tests can. Under a stated assumption, record-labeled TDH2 restores the confidentiality plain threshold ElGamal loses to parties obtaining other releases. For custodians that fail and recover, a hidden-Markov recursion gives the exact risk that a dispute fails after a given audit history, and a floor shows when auditing more often cannot help. Exact analysis, simulation and a 32-process testbed confirm these results, show that selective withholders pass every audit yet defeat every dispute, and, in a pre-registered replication, support an order-statistic deadline except without network delay.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{Dispute-key availability, threshold decryption, encrypted rollups, readiness audit, acceptance sampling, selective withholding}

\maketitle

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Optimistic rollups execute transactions off chain and accept the result unless a challenger proves it wrong within a dispute window\cite{kalodner2018arbitrum}. When the executed workload is private, as in encrypted machine-learning inference\cite{conway2024opml,eigenai2026}, the records a challenger needs are published only as ciphertexts. Data-availability mechanisms can keep these ciphertexts retrievable. They cannot ensure that the committee holding shares of the decryption key delivers enough valid decryption contributions once a dispute is authorized and before its deadline. A ciphertext that cannot be opened in time is, for the dispute, unavailable. AI-rollup disputes are our running example, but the question arises wherever a protocol must open threshold-encrypted inputs on demand.

The failure is silent until it is needed. Custodians may lose shares, fail together when a provider or region goes down, or run broken software, and the key must stay serviceable for a dispute window that lasts days and may outlive the committee that sealed the record. A strategic custodian may also answer every routine check and refuse one targeted dispute; no audit of the kind studied here can detect that, and we treat it as a limit. Threshold encryption, verifiable and proactive secret sharing, and proofs of retrievability and data-availability sampling\cite{desmedt1990threshold,feldman1987vss,schoenmakers1999pvss,herzberg1995proactive,juels2007por,albassam2021fraud} answer adjacent questions; none produces public evidence that enough custodians can serve an authorized dispute now, or states what such evidence implies.

We study this property, \emph{dispute-key availability} (DKA), and design and evaluate KEYSTONE, a readiness audit for it that targets non-strategic faults. KEYSTONE seals each record under a fresh key wrapped by a threshold Diffie--Hellman KEM. Routine audits ask a beacon-sampled subset of custodians to apply their shares to a \emph{canary}, a group element hashed from public audit context, and to prove correctness with a Chaum--Pedersen equality-of-discrete-logarithm (DLEQ) proof; each response is structurally a threshold-coin or threshold-signature share on a hashed message\cite{cachin2005constantinople,boldyreva2003threshold}. An authorized dispute applies the same share operation to the disputed record. Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{A property decomposition} (Section~\ref{sec:properties}) of $(\varepsilon,\Delta_d)$-DKA into ciphertext availability, valid-share registration, audit-time readiness, authorized decryptability, deadline liveness and pre-authorization confidentiality, with witnesses for three inferences a deployment must not draw.
  \item \textbf{A confidentiality-preserving audit} (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}) whose canary transcripts are simulatable from public shares, so audits exercise real shares without opening records. The plain threshold KEM is malleable across records; record-labeled TDH2 restores confidentiality against parties who obtain other releases.
  \item \textbf{An exact analysis} (Section~\ref{sec:analysis}): operating characteristics, showing that small audits cannot separate a committee one share short of $t$ from a live one; sample sizes and sequential tests that certify a safety margin; a placement condition; a deadline budget; and, for custodians that fail and recover, the exact posterior risk given an audit history, a frequency floor and the longest audit interval meeting a risk target.
  \item \textbf{An evaluation with labeled evidence} (Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}): exact analysis, prespecified simulation, microbenchmarks and a 32-custodian testbed with a pre-registered replication, with negative results: a high benign alarm rate under the strictest rule, a selective-withholding counterexample, deadlines missed without network delay and slower batch verification.
\end{enumerate}
None of the primitives is new, and a passed audit does not prove future availability.

Sections~\ref{sec:prelim}--\ref{sec:evaluation} give the model, properties, protocol, analysis and evaluation, and Sections~\ref{sec:discussion}--\ref{sec:conclusion} discuss them.

\section{Preliminaries}\label{sec:prelim}

\paragraph{Groups and sharing.} Let $\G$ be a cyclic group of prime order $\ell$ with generator $g$ in which the decisional Diffie--Hellman (DDH) problem is hard. The prototype uses ristretto255, a prime-order group built on Curve25519\cite{rfc9496}, and keeps the quadratic residues modulo the RFC~7919 primes\cite{rfc7919} (ffdhe2048, ffdhe3072; $\ell=(p-1)/2$, $g=4$) as a baseline; we write groups multiplicatively, and $q$ denotes only the acceptance threshold of an audit, and $\binom{a}{b}=0$ when $b>a$ or $b<0$. A secret $x\in\Zq$ is Shamir-shared with a polynomial $f$ of degree $t-1$, $f(0)=x$; custodian $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ holds $x_i=f(i)$ and publishes $Y_i=g^{x_i}$\cite{shamir1979share}, verifiable against Feldman commitments\cite{feldman1987vss}. Any $t$ distinct indices $I$ have Lagrange coefficients $\lambda_i^I$ with $\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i^I x_i=x$.

\paragraph{Threshold Diffie--Hellman KEM.} With epoch key $PK=g^{x}$, a sender draws $\rho\leftarrow\Zq$, publishes $C_1=g^{\rho}$ and derives a key-encryption key from $PK^{\rho}$ and the record identifier. Any $t$ partial decryptions $C_1^{x_i}$ determine $C_1^{x}=\prod_{i\in I}(C_1^{x_i})^{\lambda_i^I}$. This threshold ElGamal KEM\cite{desmedt1990threshold} is semantically secure under DDH in the random-oracle model but malleable: anyone can turn $C_1$ into $C_1g^{\gamma}$. Shoup and Gennaro's TDH2 binds a label and a proof of knowledge of $\rho$ to the ciphertext, which makes it secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks\cite{shoup2002securing}; KEYSTONE uses it for disputes (Section~\ref{sec:conf}).

\paragraph{DLEQ proofs, hashing and beacon.} A Chaum--Pedersen proof\cite{chaum1992dleq} shows $\log_g Y_i=\log_X D_i$: the prover picks $\nu\leftarrow\Zq$, sends $a_1=g^{\nu}$, $a_2=X^{\nu}$, derives $c=H(g,Y_i,X,D_i,a_1,a_2,\mathsf{ctx})$ by the Fiat--Shamir transform\cite{fiat1987prove} and returns $z=\nu+c\,x_i$; the verifier checks $g^{z}=a_1Y_i^{c}$ and $X^{z}=a_2D_i^{c}$. The request context $\mathsf{ctx}$ ties each proof to one request. $H_G$ maps byte strings to $\G\setminus\{1\}$ with domain separation; we model $H$ and $H_G$ as random oracles. A public beacon outputs values that are unpredictable before publication\cite{das2022spurt}.

% =====================================================================
\section{System and threat model}\label{sec:model}

An epoch $E$ has $n$ custodians placed in failure domains (providers, regions, software stacks), a threshold $t$, a key $PK_E$ and registered public shares $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$. A rollup worker encrypts each record $r$ under a fresh data key $K_r$ with AES-GCM, wraps $K_r$ under the KEM, and publishes the result to a data-availability (DA) layer. A settlement layer, the \emph{bulletin board}, records registrations, requests, deadlines and evidence and supplies an ordered public clock. A \emph{combiner} inside the authorized destination collects partial decryptions over authenticated, confidential channels; it learns $K_r$ for records it may open and is trusted not to disclose it. The board stores only commitments to responses with their validity status and timestamps, never enough to decrypt a record; canary responses may be public (Lemma~\ref{lem:sim}). Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} shows the three paths.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_architecture.pdf}
\caption{KEYSTONE architecture. Sealing, routine canary auditing and authorized dispute release are separate paths over one custodian committee. The audit uses a beacon-derived canary, never a production ciphertext; only an authorized dispute requests partial decryptions of a record's KEM component $C_1$. Dashed arrows are public evidence written to the bulletin board.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure}

\begin{assumption}[Threshold confidentiality]\label{as:conf}
During an epoch the adversary learns fewer than $t$ current shares. DDH is hard in $\G$; $H$, $H_G$ and the key-derivation function are independent, domain-separated random oracles; and AES-GCM is a secure authenticated-encryption scheme.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Beacon]\label{as:beacon}
An audit's beacon value is unpredictable until its epoch, slot and committee are committed on the bulletin board, and the derived sample is uniform (without replacement, or within each domain quota for stratified samples) and independent of other audits' samples. The prototype derives the sample with a SHA-256 counter stream and rejection sampling, which we model as ideal.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Bulletin board and data availability]\label{as:board}
The bulletin board is append-only and totally ordered and exposes each request to custodians within $\delta_b$. The DA layer keeps committed ciphertexts and receipts retrievable, and record identifiers are unique.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Bounded delay, for deadline statements only]\label{as:sync}
Messages between non-faulty parties arrive within $\delta$ over channels that authenticate the sending custodian. A non-faulty custodian produces a partial decryption with proof within $c_p$; the combiner verifies one proof within $c_v$ and combines $t$ partials within $c_c$.
\end{assumption}

Detection and confidentiality statements do not use Assumption~\ref{as:sync}. The adversary may crash custodians individually or by domain, cause share loss, send invalid or equivocal responses, issue unauthorized requests, act as a worker that commits records of its choice and obtains their releases, and control \emph{selective} custodians that answer canaries but withhold targeted dispute responses. Corruption is static within an epoch. Out of scope are production key-generation security, combiners or verifiers that leak records they may open, arbitrary asynchronous partitions, and selective withholding beyond Observation~\ref{prop:nonimpl}. An audit shows that whoever answered knows $x_i$, not that the registered operator does, so share pooling and false domain declarations are invisible to it; and threshold custody replaces the one-honest-challenger assumption of optimistic rollups with an assumption on $t$ of $n$ custodians.

% =====================================================================
\section{Dispute-key availability}\label{sec:properties}

Fix an epoch $E$, a record $r$ with KEM component $C_1$, and a request time $\tau$ on the bulletin board.

\begin{definition}[Ciphertext availability]\label{def:ca}
$\CA(r,\tau)$ holds if the committed encrypted record and its receipt are retrievable from the DA layer at $\tau$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Valid-share registration]\label{def:vsr}
$\VSR(E)$ holds if the registered public shares are consistent with one degree-$(t-1)$ polynomial whose constant term is the epoch secret, and every admitted custodian initially received the matching share.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Readiness]\label{def:ready}
For a request $\mathsf{req}$, an audit or a dispute on a named record, $\Ready_i(E,\tau,\mathsf{req},\Delta)=1$ if custodian $i$ can access its current share, perform the requested operation, produce a valid DLEQ proof and deliver the response by $\tau+\Delta$. Audit readiness and dispute readiness for each record are distinct predicates.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Audit-time readiness]\label{def:akr}
For a sample $S$ of $s$ custodians and threshold $q\le s$, $\AKR(E,S,\tau)$ holds if at least $q$ members of $S$ deliver valid canary responses by the audit deadline.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Authorized decryptability and deadline liveness]\label{def:ad}
After a valid authorization for $r$ at $\tau$, $\AD(r,E,\tau)$ holds if the combiner obtains valid partial decryptions of $C_1$ from at least $t$ distinct custodians, and $\DDL(r,E,\tau,\Delta_d)$ holds if this happens by $\tau+\Delta_d$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Pre-authorization confidentiality]\label{def:pac}
$\PAC$ holds for $r$ if no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary that satisfies Assumption~\ref{as:conf}, chooses two equal-length plaintexts for $r$ and observes the sealed record and all audit transcripts, but no dispute releases, guesses which plaintext was sealed with non-negligible advantage. In the stronger $\PAC^{+}$, the adversary may also commit records of its choice and obtain the release of every record other than $r$, where a \emph{release} is the set of partial decryptions and the combined value delivered to the authorized destination, which the adversary may control for its own records.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dispute-key availability]\label{def:dka}
Fix a readiness model, a distribution over custodian failures, share loss and message delays over time. An epoch provides $(\varepsilon,\Delta_d)$-$\DKA$ under it if for every committed record $r$ and authorization time $\tau$, $\Pr[\DDL(r,E,\tau,\Delta_d)]\ge 1-\varepsilon$ over the readiness model and the protocol's randomness, and $\PAC^{+}$ holds for every record before its authorization.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Catastrophic state and detection]\label{def:fa}
An epoch is \emph{catastrophic} at $\tau$ if fewer than $t$ custodians are audit-ready. An audit \emph{falsely accepts} if $\AKR$ holds in a catastrophic state; its \emph{detection probability} is one minus its false-accept probability. Dispute readiness can be lower than audit readiness (Observation~\ref{prop:nonimpl}).
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Timescale and epochs]
Dispute windows last days and interactive moves hours, so DKA chiefly requires the key to stay serviceable throughout the window, while $\Delta_d$ matters for per-move timers. A record stays disputable after its committee rotates, so old committees must stay serviceable, or hand over shares by dynamic proactive sharing\cite{maram2019churp,yurek2023dpss}, and audits must cover every epoch with open records.
\end{remark}

The next observation records what the weaker properties do not imply; each elementary witness blocks a tempting inference.

\begin{observation}[Non-implications]\label{prop:nonimpl}
Fix $1\le t\le n$, $1\le q\le s\le n$ and $\Delta_d$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\CA(r,\tau)$ does not imply $\DDL(r,E,\tau,\Delta_d)$.
  \item $\AKR(E,S,\tau)$ does not imply $\AD(r,E,\tau')$ for an authorized dispute at $\tau'\ge\tau$.
  \item For every $m$, $m$ accepted audits at times $\tau_1<\dots<\tau_m$ do not imply $\AD(r,E,\tau')$ for $\tau'>\tau_m$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{observation}

\begin{proof}
(1) Let the DA layer retain the record while exactly $t-1$ custodians are dispute-ready for $r$ and the others have lost their shares. $\CA$ holds, but at most $t-1$ valid partials exist, so $\AD$ and $\DDL$ fail.
(2) Let all custodians be audit-ready and let $n-t+1$ of them answer every canary but withhold every response for $r$: $\AKR$ holds for every $S$, while at most $t-1$ custodians answer the dispute.
(3) Take two executions with all custodians audit-ready up to $\tau_m$; afterwards all stay ready in the first and $n-t+1$ lose their shares in the second. The audit histories are identical but $\AD$ holds at $\tau'$ only in the first, so without a model of how readiness evolves no predicate of the history implies $\AD$.
\end{proof}

Item~(2) is why audit and dispute readiness are separate predicates; item~(3) is why a repeated-audit guarantee needs a temporal model, static (Corollary~\ref{cor:repeat}) or stochastic (Section~\ref{sec:temporal}).

\section{The KEYSTONE protocol}\label{sec:protocol}

\paragraph{Setup and sealing.} The committee is formed under identity, stake and failure-domain placement policy (Observation~\ref{prop:cap}). A deployment would use an authenticated distributed key generation or publicly verifiable secret sharing\cite{gennaro2007dkg,das2022adkg,schoenmakers1999pvss}; the prototype uses a dealer with Feldman commitments as an explicit substitution boundary. To seal $r$ under the label $L_r=(E,\mathsf{id}_r,\text{policy hash})$, the worker draws $\rho$, computes $C_1=g^{\rho}$ and $\kappa=\mathrm{KDF}(PK_E^{\rho},L_r)$, wraps $K_r$ under $\kappa$, adds a TDH2 proof that binds $L_r$ and the wrapped key to $C_1$\cite{shoup2002securing}, encrypts the record under $K_r$ with AES-GCM, and publishes the envelope with its DA pointer.

\paragraph{Readiness audit.} The coordinator commits an epoch and audit slot. The next finalized beacon value $\beta$ fixes a sample $S$ of $s$ custodians, uniform or stratified by domain, and everyone derives the canary $X=H_G(\texttt{KEYSTONE-CANARY}\parallel E\parallel \mathsf{slot}\parallel \beta)$. Each sampled custodian returns $D_i=X^{x_i}$ with a DLEQ proof that $\log_g Y_i=\log_X D_i$, bound to the request context and its index. The verifier checks membership, freshness, uniqueness per index, proof validity and the deadline, and accepts after $q$ valid responses.

\paragraph{Authorized dispute.} A dispute starts once the policy contract binds a record, epoch, authorized verifier and deadline $\Delta_d$. Each custodian checks the authorization, the TDH2 proof and that the label is the authorized record's, and returns $C_1^{x_i}$ with a DLEQ proof bound to the dispute. The combiner verifies responses on arrival, off its network event loop, discards duplicates and invalid ones, stops at $t$ valid partials, interpolates $C_1^{x}=PK_E^{\rho}$, re-derives $\kappa$, unwraps $K_r$ and decrypts.

\paragraph{Transcript and evidence.} For each request, the board records commitments to valid, invalid, equivocal, stale and unauthorized responses and the absence of missing ones, with timestamps. Invalid proofs and conflicting responses are self-contained cryptographic evidence; attributing a missing response to a custodian additionally requires Assumption~\ref{as:sync}. The prototype contract is a skeleton: an administrator supplies the sample and canary hash when opening an audit without an on-chain beacon check, records invalid-response evidence after off-chain verification, and can cancel requests. Theorem~\ref{thm:fa} therefore holds for the prototype only if the administrator samples as the protocol prescribes; deriving the sample on chain from the committed beacon and verifying proofs on chain are needed for a trustless deployment.

\subsection{Security of the audit}

\begin{lemma}[Correctness and knowledge soundness]\label{lem:correct}
An honest response passes verification. In the random-oracle model a verifying response satisfies $D_i=X^{x_i}$ except with negligible probability, and the proof is a proof of knowledge: from any party that produces verifying responses for fresh canaries with non-negligible probability, an extractor obtains $x_i$. Any $t$ verified partials of $C_1$ with distinct indices $I$ combine to $\prod_{i\in I}(C_1^{x_i})^{\lambda_i^I}=PK_E^{\rho}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Completeness and combination are direct computations. The protocol is special-sound, and with the Fiat--Shamir hash as a random oracle the forking lemma yields an extractor\cite{chaum1992dleq,fiat1987prove}. Full proofs of Lemmas~\ref{lem:correct}--\ref{lem:subst} are in the supplementary material.
\end{proof}

Knowledge soundness makes a passed audit meaningful: whoever passes canary audits with non-negligible probability holds $x_i$, and under Assumption~\ref{as:conf} the adversary cannot obtain an honest custodian's share from public values without solving a discrete logarithm.

\begin{lemma}[Audit transcripts are simulatable]\label{lem:sim}
Model $H_G$ and $H$ as random oracles. A simulator that knows only $g$ and $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ answers all queries to $H_G$ and $H$ and produces the honest custodians' audit responses $(X,(D_i,\pi_i)_{i\in S})$ for any audit context and any $S$, including $S=\{1,\dots,n\}$. With at most $N$ simulated proofs and $Q$ oracle queries, simulated and real views are within statistical distance $NQ/\ell$, so observing audits changes any adversary's advantage against $\PAC$ by at most $2NQ/\ell$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The simulator answers each fresh $H_G$ query with $g^{a}$ for a stored random $a$, so for an honest custodian and canary $X=g^{a}$ it can output the real response $D_i=Y_i^{a}=X^{x_i}$, and it produces each proof with the honest-verifier zero-knowledge simulator, programming $H$; a programmed input was queried before with probability at most $Q/\ell$. Domain separation keeps this programming apart from a KEM reduction that programs the key-derivation oracle.
\end{proof}

This is the standard simulation argument for threshold-coin and threshold-signature shares on hashed messages\cite{cachin2005constantinople,boldyreva2003threshold}, which we restate for the audit setting. Lemma~\ref{lem:sim} holds even for adversarially chosen audit contexts and beacons. It is why the audit can exercise every sampled share without opening any record: combining $t$ canary partials yields $X^{x}$ for a hash-derived $X$, which equals a fixed record component only with negligible probability.

\begin{lemma}[No production substitution]\label{lem:subst}
Model $H_G$ as a random oracle. For a fixed $C_1$, a coordinator making $Q$ queries to $H_G$ finds an audit context whose canary equals $C_1$ with probability at most $Q/(\ell-1)$, by a union bound over uniform oracle answers.
\end{lemma}

\begin{remark}
The prototype hashes to ristretto255 with the standard map from a 64-byte hash\cite{rfc9496}; the ffdhe baseline uses \texttt{expand\_message\_xmd}\cite{rfc9380} before squaring. Binding request context into the Fiat--Shamir hash does not give the share isolation of context-dependent threshold decryption\cite{boneh2025context}, and the lemmas do not cover side channels.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Confidentiality against releases of other records}\label{sec:conf}

Lemma~\ref{lem:sim} concerns audits only. An adversary that can also obtain releases, for example a worker that commits and disputes its own records, defeats the plain KEM.

\begin{proposition}[Malleability across records]\label{prop:malleable}
With the plain threshold Diffie--Hellman KEM, $\PAC^{+}$ does not hold: an adversary that obtains the release of one record of its choice recovers $K_r$ for any target record $r$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For the target's component $C_1$, the adversary commits a record $r'$ with $C_1'=C_1g^{\gamma}$ and obtains its release $C_1'^{x}=C_1^{x}PK_E^{\gamma}$. It computes $PK_E^{\rho}=C_1^{x}=C_1'^{x}PK_E^{-\gamma}$, derives the target's key-encryption key from $PK_E^{\rho}$ and the target's public record identifier and metadata, and unwraps $K_r$. Already $\gamma=0$, re-submitting $C_1$ under a new identifier, suffices.
\end{proof}

The attack does not involve the audit. It is blocked by a threshold KEM whose custodians refuse components not bound to the authorized record, such as TDH2 with the record label\cite{shoup2002securing} or context-dependent threshold decryption\cite{boneh2025context}; KEYSTONE uses TDH2.

\begin{assumption}[TDH2 key encapsulation]\label{as:tdh2}
TDH2 used as a key-encapsulation mechanism, with $\kappa=\mathrm{KDF}(PK_E^{\rho},L)$ in place of a one-time pad, is secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks in the threshold model of Shoup and Gennaro, who prove this for the encryption scheme under DDH in the random-oracle model\cite{shoup2002securing}.
\end{assumption}

\begin{lemma}[Record-bound releases]\label{lem:pacplus}
Let the dispute KEM be TDH2 with label $L_r$, and let each custodian release $C_1^{x_i}$ only for a ciphertext whose TDH2 proof verifies and whose label is the authorized one. Under Assumptions~\ref{as:conf} and~\ref{as:tdh2} and static corruption, $\PAC^{+}$ holds for every record, and Lemma~\ref{lem:sim} continues to hold.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A release of a record $r'\neq r$ answers a decryption-share query for a valid ciphertext with label $L_{r'}\neq L_r$. Because the label enters the TDH2 proof, a re-labelled or mauled $C_1$ either fails verification and is refused, or is a valid ciphertext other than the challenge, which the chosen-ciphertext game of Assumption~\ref{as:tdh2} answers. The target's key-encryption key is therefore pseudorandom, and AES-GCM hides the wrapped key and then the record. The canary path is unchanged and its oracles are domain separated, so the simulation of Lemma~\ref{lem:sim} composes with the TDH2 reduction.
\end{proof}

The cost is one ciphertext-proof check per custodian per dispute (\RtwoCtCheckRis\,ms in ristretto255, Table~\ref{tab:operations}). The prototype's custodians enforce both checks, and a test reproduces the attack of Proposition~\ref{prop:malleable} once they are removed.

\section{Analysis}\label{sec:analysis}

\begin{theorem}[False-accept probability]\label{thm:fa}
Suppose exactly $k$ custodians are audit-ready throughout one audit, the sample $S$ of size $s$ is uniform without replacement and independent of readiness (Assumption~\ref{as:beacon}), and acceptance requires $q$ valid responses. Then, up to the negligible soundness error of Lemma~\ref{lem:correct},
\begin{equation}
\Pr[\mathsf{accept}\mid k]=\sum_{j=q}^{\min(s,k)}\frac{\binom{k}{j}\binom{n-k}{s-j}}{\binom{n}{s}}.
\label{eq:hypergeom}
\end{equation}
This is non-decreasing in $k$, so over catastrophic states ($k\le t-1$) it is maximized at $k=t-1$, and for $q=s$
\begin{equation}
\varepsilon_a=\max_{k<t}\Pr[\mathsf{accept}\mid k]=\frac{\binom{t-1}{s}}{\binom{n}{s}}.
\label{eq:bound}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The number of ready custodians in $S$ is hypergeometric $(n,k,s)$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:correct} the audit accepts exactly when it is at least $q$, up to negligible error. If $R\subset R'$, then $|S\cap R|\le|S\cap R'|$ for every $S$, which gives monotonicity; for $q=s$ only $j=s$ contributes.
\end{proof}

For $n=32$, $t=22$, $s=q=8$, $\varepsilon_a=\binom{21}{8}/\binom{32}{8}=203{,}490/10{,}518{,}300=0.0193$, so a single audit detects the worst catastrophic state with probability $0.9807$ under a static, non-selective fault model. Section~\ref{sec:oc} shows why this number alone is misleading. Supplementary Figure~S1 shows detection against $s$.

\begin{corollary}[Repeated audits under a static state]\label{cor:repeat}
If the ready set is fixed and catastrophic for $m$ audits whose samples are independent (Assumption~\ref{as:beacon}), all $m$ falsely accept with probability at most $\varepsilon_a^{m}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Given the fixed ready set, the acceptance events are independent, each with probability at most $\varepsilon_a$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:fa}.
\end{proof}

By Observation~\ref{prop:nonimpl}(3), the static hypothesis cannot be dropped without a temporal model.

For samples stratified by domain, the per-domain counts of ready sampled custodians are independent hypergeometric variables, so acceptance is the probability that their sum reaches $q$ (supplementary Proposition~S1); the worst catastrophic state then depends on how the $t-1$ ready custodians are spread across domains.

\begin{observation}[Placement cap]\label{prop:cap}
With no failures other than whole-domain outages, no single domain outage prevents reconstruction if and only if every domain has at most $n-t$ custodians, since an outage of a domain of size $d$ leaves $n-d$.
\end{observation}

The baseline places four domains of eight under the cap $n-t=10$: one outage is survivable, two leave $16<22$ custodians.

\begin{observation}[Benign pass probability]\label{prop:benign}
If each custodian is independently unavailable with probability $f$ and the sample is independent of availability, the audit passes with probability $\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(s,1-f)\ge q]$, since the sampled custodians' availability indicators are independent.
\end{observation}

The strict rule $q=s$ that maximizes detection also turns every benign miss into an alarm. For $s=q=8$ and $f=0.10$ a healthy committee passes only with probability $0.9^{8}=0.430$, although $t$ of 32 shares are reachable with probability $\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(32,0.9)\ge 22]=0.99983$. Table~\ref{tab:acceptance} and supplementary Figure~S2 give the trade-off. At $s=8$, $q=7$ lowers detection to \RAccEightSevenDet{} and raises the benign pass rate at $f=0.10$ only to \RAccEightSevenPass{}; a larger sample helps: $s=16$, $q=14$ detects \RAccSixteenFourteenDet{} with benign pass rates of \RAccSixteenFourteenPassFive{} at $f=0.05$ and \RAccSixteenFourteenPassTen{} at $f=0.10$. This post hoc analysis is design guidance, not a prespecified result.

\subsection{Operating characteristic and sequential audits}\label{sec:oc}

Worst-case detection hides how weak a small audit is near the threshold. Table~\ref{tab:oc} gives the exact operating characteristic: with $s=q=8$ the audit accepts a committee one share short of $t$ with probability \OcEightTwentyOne{}, a live committee with no spare share with \OcEightTwentyTwo{}, and one with four spare shares with only \OcEightTwentySix{}. Only the full probe ($s=n$) separates $k=t-1$ from $k=t$ at 5\% error rates, so sampled guarantees must be stated for a safety margin $m$, testing $k\le t-1$ against $k\ge t+m$. With error rates of 5\% each, a single audit needs $s=\SepSFour$ ($q=\SepQFour$) for $m=4$, $s=\SepSSix$ ($q=\SepQSix$) for $m=6$ and $s=\SepSEight$ ($q=\SepQEight$) for $m=8$. A sequential probability ratio test across audits\cite{wald1945sprt}, valid under the static state of Corollary~\ref{cor:repeat}, is far cheaper: for $m=6$ it decides on average after \AsnSixteenDead{} audits for a failed committee and \AsnSixteenLive{} for a live one with $s=16$, $q=14$, and after \AsnEightDead{} and \AsnEightLive{} with $s=q=8$ (Wald's approximations). Audits should therefore be specified by the margin they certify and their error rates, not by worst-case detection.

\begin{proposition}[Deadline budget]\label{prop:budget}
Under Assumptions~\ref{as:board} and~\ref{as:sync}, suppose at least $t$ custodians are non-faulty, hold their shares and follow the protocol, and the combiner is work-conserving, verifies serially and verifies each authenticated index at most once. Then a dispute requested at $\tau$ obtains $t$ valid partials by $\tau+\delta_b+c_p+\delta+n\,c_v$, and the key is recovered $c_c$ later. Hence $\Delta_d\ge\delta_b+c_p+\delta+n\,c_v$ suffices for $\DDL$, and $n\,c_v$ may be replaced by $t\,c_v$ if no invalid response precedes the $t$-th valid one.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each of the $t$ correct custodians' responses arrives by $T'=\tau+\delta_b+c_p+\delta$. Authenticated channels stop an adversary from occupying a correct custodian's index, so the work-conserving combiner verifies at most $n$ responses and finishes by $T'+n\,c_v$, or by $T'+t\,c_v$ if no invalid response comes first.
\end{proof}

On a production settlement layer, $\delta_b$ is a block or finality time and can dominate. With random delays, a per-message quantile for $\delta$ does not budget for the slowest of the $t$ responses needed:

\begin{corollary}[Stochastic deadline]\label{cor:os}
Suppose $n_\ell$ custodians can answer, each response is delivered independently with probability $p_\ell$ after a round trip with distribution function $F$, and the combiner finishes within $B$ after the $t$-th valid response. Then $\Pr[\DDL(r,E,\tau,\Delta_d)]\ge\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n_\ell,p_\ell F(\Delta_d-B))\ge t]$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The number of responses delivered within $\Delta_d-B$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(n_\ell,p_\ell F(\Delta_d-B))$; if it reaches $t$, the dispute completes by $\Delta_d$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Readiness over time}\label{sec:temporal}

We now let custodians fail and recover. Each custodian is an independent two-state Markov chain with failure rate $\phi$ and repair rate $\psi$, so it is up a fraction $v=\psi/(\phi+\psi)$ of the time; in a variant, each of four domains of eight also fails as a unit at rate $\phi_d$ and recovers at rate $\psi_d$. Audits run every $T$ with a fresh uniform sample and only observe: they trigger no repair. Faults are non-selective, so a custodian is audit-ready exactly when it is dispute-ready, and disputes arrive independently of the process. Let $Z(\tau)$ be the number of ready custodians, $A(k)$ the acceptance probability of Eq.~\eqref{eq:hypergeom}, $\omega$ the stationary law of $Z$, and $\mathbf{1}_{<t}$ the indicator column of $Z<t$; vectors are rows over $k\in\{0,\dots,n\}$.

\begin{theorem}[Risk given an audit history]\label{thm:hmm}
$Z$ is a Markov chain with $P_u(k,k')=\sum_i \mathrm{b}(i;k,p_{\uparrow}(u))\,\mathrm{b}(k'-i;n-k,p_{\downarrow}(u))$, where $\mathrm{b}$ is the binomial mass function, $p_{\uparrow}(u)=v+(1-v)e^{-(\phi+\psi)u}$ and $p_{\downarrow}(u)=v(1-e^{-(\phi+\psi)u})$. For audit outcomes $o_1,\dots,o_j$, let $\alpha_1\propto\omega\odot e_{o_1}$ and $\alpha_i\propto(\alpha_{i-1}P_T)\odot e_{o_i}$, normalized, with $e_{\mathsf{acc}}=A$ and $e_{\mathsf{rej}}=1-A$. A dispute at $jT+u$, $0\le u<T$, fails to reach $t$ with probability $\alpha_jP_u\mathbf{1}_{<t}$ given $o_1,\dots,o_j$. With domain shocks, the same holds for the chain of per-domain pairs (domain up, members up).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
From any configuration with $k$ custodians up, after time $u$ each up custodian is up with probability $p_{\uparrow}(u)$ and each down one with $p_{\downarrow}(u)$, independently, so $Z$ is strongly lumpable with kernel $P_u$. A fresh uniform sample makes each outcome conditionally independent of everything else given $Z$ at its audit, with emission $A$, so the history is a hidden Markov model and the recursion is the forward algorithm.
\end{proof}

After an unbroken run of accepted audits, $\alpha_j$ converges from any start to the normalized Perron vector $\alpha^{*}$ of $P_T\,\mathrm{diag}(A)$ on the states the audit can accept, where it is entrywise positive for $T>0$. We call $R(T)=\sup_{0\le u<T}\alpha^{*}P_u\mathbf{1}_{<t}$ the \emph{posterior risk}: the failure probability a dispute faces, at the worst point of an audit cycle, after a long clean audit record.

\begin{theorem}[Undetected failure]\label{thm:floor}
Let $U(T)=\frac1T\int_0^T(\omega\odot A)P_u\mathbf{1}_{<t}\,du$, the long-run probability that a dispute fails and the most recent audit accepted. With or without domain shocks, $U$ is non-decreasing in $T$ and $U(T)\ge U_0=\sum_{k<t}\omega(k)A(k)$, its limit as $T\to0$. Without domain shocks,
\[
U(T)\le A(t-1)\,\omega(Z<t)+\sum_{k\ge t}\omega(k)A(k)\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(k,p_{\uparrow}(T))<t].
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The chain is reversible, moves one custodian or domain at a time, and is stochastically monotone because $p_{\uparrow}\ge p_{\downarrow}$. Let $g(u)=(\omega\odot A)P_u\mathbf{1}_{<t}$. Then $g'(u)$ is minus the Dirichlet form of $A$ and $P_u\mathbf{1}_{<t}$; $A$ is increasing and $P_u$ keeps $\mathbf{1}_{<t}$ decreasing, so every term has the sign that makes $g'\ge0$. Hence $U$, the mean of $g$ over $[0,T]$, is non-decreasing and at least $g(0)=U_0$. For the bound, use $A(k)\le A(t-1)$ for $k<t$, and for $k\ge t$ note that the custodians up at the audit and still up at $u$ number $\mathrm{Bin}(k,p_{\uparrow}(u))$, lower-bound $Z(u)$, and decrease in $u$.
\end{proof}

Since audits trigger no repair, the failure probability itself is $\omega(Z<t)$; $U$ measures how much of it the latest audit fails to flag. A target $\varepsilon<U_0$ cannot be met by auditing more often, only by a stronger design or a larger availability margin. Otherwise the longest admissible interval $T^{*}(\varepsilon)=\sup\{T:U(T)\le\varepsilon\}$ is the cheapest schedule, found by bisection because $U$ is monotone, and the bound gives a conservative interval in closed form. Full proofs are in the supplementary material.

\section{Evaluation}\label{sec:evaluation}

We compare the audit with simpler checks (Q1), separate audit outcomes from dispute success under failures (Q2), test deadline liveness (Q3), measure cost (Q4) and evaluate readiness over time (Q5).

\paragraph{Method.} Table~\ref{tab:config} lists every experiment, and each result carries one of four evidence labels. \emph{Exact} values are closed forms or recursions under a declared model. \emph{Simulation} results come from cells whose parameters, endpoints and seeds were fixed and hashed before execution; the three Q2 cells have 131{,}072 draws each, above the 73{,}778 that Hoeffding's inequality requires for a proportion's half-width of 0.005 at 95\% confidence\cite{hoeffding1963}, and where an exact value exists simulation serves as an implementation check. \emph{Microbenchmarks} are single-process medians, and \emph{emulation} runs 32 custodian processes on one host. A first prototype (R1: ffdhe2048, serial verification on the network loop) produced Q1, Q2 and the comparison column of Q3; the second (R2: ristretto255, TDH2, verification off the loop) followed a second design hashed before any R2 run. Proportions carry 95\% Wilson intervals\cite{wilson1927}.

\subsection{Readiness baselines (Q1)}

A heartbeat is answered even by a custodian that lost its share, registration is checked once, and decrypting a real record discloses it (supplementary Table~S4 compares these checks). A full-committee canary probe ($s=n$) detects every static catastrophic state at four times KEYSTONE's cost and is affordable once per epoch at $n=32$. Sampling pays off when audits are frequent, committees are large or responses are recorded on chain: at 57{,}882 gas per response (supplementary Table~S2), responses cost about $0.46$ million gas per audit for $s=8$ and $1.85$ million for $s=32$.

\subsection{Robustness under failures (Q2)}\label{sec:eval-robust}

In the simulation cells (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}), 10\% independent unavailability leaves the committee reconstructable in \RIIDRecon{} of draws while the strict audit passes in only \RIIDAudit{}: a sensitive alarm, not a health score. Under 20\% domain outages, stratified sampling raised conditional detection of catastrophic draws from \RStratDetU{} to \RStratDetS{} and lowered the benign pass rate from \RStratPassU{} to \RStratPassS{}. The prespecified endpoint, the paired difference in detected catastrophes per draw, was \RStratD{} with Hoeffding half-width \RStratHW{}, too conservative to resolve an effect this small; a post hoc exact sign test on the \RStratDiscordant{} discordant pairs, all favoring stratification, gives $p=\McNemarP$. With eleven selective withholders, audits passed in \RSWAudit{} of draws and disputes succeeded in \RSWDispute{}, reproducing the witness of Observation~\ref{prop:nonimpl}(2).

\subsection{Deadline liveness in an emulated testbed (Q3)}\label{sec:eval-deadline}

Thirty-two custodian processes, each a TCP server holding only its own ristretto255 share, and one combiner run on one host. Each trace runs one canary audit ($s=q=8$) and one dispute over a fresh 1\,KiB record; the combiner verifies DLEQ proofs in a worker thread and stops at $t=22$ valid partials. Delays are lognormal on both legs, lost messages are not retransmitted, and crashed custodians never answer. Two runs of eight profiles $\times$ \RtwoTraces{} traces $\times$ two verification variants used different deadlines (Table~\ref{tab:testbed}). R2 used $\Delta_d^{*}=c_p+2\delta_{99}+t\,c_v+c_c$, Proposition~\ref{prop:budget} with each leg's 99th-percentile delay and the medians of Table~\ref{tab:operations}, fixed before its run. R2b, designed after R2 and fixed before any of its traces, used fresh seeds shared by both variants and the deadline $\Delta_{os}$ at which Corollary~\ref{cor:os} gives 0.99, with $B$ calibrated below.

\paragraph{R2.} Five of the seven reconstructable profiles succeeded in every trace, and eleven crashes ($21<t$) defeated every dispute. With delay, completion followed the network, with medians from \RtwoMedLo{} to \RtwoMedHi\,ms, against \RDLMedLo--\RDLMedHi\,s in R1, where serial verification on the network loop took about 3\,s. Two profiles missed. Without delay, no dispute met the \RtwoControlDstar\,ms deadline (median \RtwoControlMed\,ms): the formula counts cryptographic work only, not message handling among 33 processes. With ten crashes all 22 survivors must answer, so the slowest of 22 round trips decides: \RtwoCrashTenSerial{} and \RtwoCrashTenBatch{} succeeded, and Corollary~\ref{cor:os} with the frozen parameters, applied post hoc, predicts \RtwoDfourPred.

\paragraph{Calibration and R2b.} On the same harness without cryptography, 22 responses took \RtwobNullMed\,ms at the median, \RtwobHandoffUs\,$\mu$s of it per hand-off to the verification thread; the full dispute path without delay took \RtwobCalibMed\,ms, with 99th percentile $B=\RtwobBzero$\,ms. In R2b, serial verification met the criterion, a Wilson upper bound of at least 0.99, in \RtwobMeets{} of eight profiles, although $\Delta_{os}$ is far tighter than $\Delta_d^{*}$ (\RtwobOsGlobal{} against \RtwoGlobalDstar\,ms under global delay), and at the R2 deadline the ten-crash profile again succeeded in \RtwobDfourAtDstar. It missed without delay: \RtwobControlRate{} \RtwobControlWilson, as the median rose from \RtwobCalibMed{} to \RtwobControlMed\,ms between runs, so a deadline without network slack is fragile to small host drift.

\paragraph{Batch verification.} In the paired R2b design, batch verification was \RtwobBatchSlowLo--\RtwobBatchSlowHi\,ms slower at the median in every delayed profile (sign tests, $p<\RtwobSignPBound$), plausibly because it starts only after the last needed arrival while serial verification overlaps with arrivals, and \RtwobBatchFastZero\,ms faster without delay, where responses arrive together and it saves hand-offs. It therefore met the control deadline (\RtwobControlBatch) but missed the regional one (\RtwobRegionalBatch), contrary to the expected absence of a difference. Audit pass rates fell inside the Wilson interval of their exact expectation in \RtwoAuditInside{} and \RtwobAuditInside{} of 16 profile and variant pairs.

\subsection{Readiness over time (Q5)}\label{sec:eval-temporal}

We evaluated Theorems~\ref{thm:hmm} and~\ref{thm:floor} on a synthetic grid of \TmpGridCells{} cells (Table~\ref{tab:config}); Table~\ref{tab:temporal} shows five scenarios. The bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:floor} held in all \TmpBoundCells{} shock-free cells. An event simulation without closed forms matched \TmpSimInfoPass{} of the \TmpSimInfo{} quantities with observed events within 99\% Wilson intervals (\TmpSimVacuous{} more, near $10^{-16}$, saw no events). Three findings stand out. First, correlated failures dominate: with custodian MTBF 30\,d and MTTR 6\,h, $\Pr[Z<t]$ is $\TmpCatIID$ for independent custodians and $\TmpCatShock$ when each domain fails every 90 days on average. Second, the floor binds: with domain shocks, custodian MTBF 7\,d and MTTR 24\,h, $U_0=\TmpFloorHard$ for $(8,8)$, so no audit interval reaches $\varepsilon=10^{-4}$, and $(24,20)$ reaches it only with audits every \TmpHardWideMin{} minutes, at the edge of the searched range. Third, larger samples are not uniformly better: $(24,20)$ lowers the floor by orders of magnitude, yet its $U$ exceeds that of $(8,8)$ in all \TmpShockTotal{} shock cells and \TmpIidWorse{} of \TmpIidTotal{} shock-free ones, each time because it accepts more often; $U$ ignores the benign alarms the strict rule raises instead. For independent custodians with MTBF 7\,d, MTTR 24\,h and $(8,8)$, the longest interval for $\varepsilon=10^{-4}$ is \TmpExactIntervalIID\,h under $U$, \TmpPostIntervalIID\,h under the posterior risk $R$, and a conservative \TmpBoundIntervalIID\,h from the bound.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

Five design consequences follow. First, specify audits by the safety margin they certify, with error rates at $k\le t-1$ and $k\ge t+m$ (Section~\ref{sec:oc}). Second, placement under the cap $n-t$ matters more than the sampling policy, and correlated domain failures dominate the risk over time (Q5). Third, schedule audits from a risk target: Theorem~\ref{thm:floor} gives the longest admissible interval, and below the floor $U_0$ only a stronger design helps. Fourth, deadlines must budget for the ledger delay, host overhead and the slowest of the $t$ needed responses (Corollary~\ref{cor:os}), not a per-message quantile; with elliptic-curve verification off the network loop, the network governs completion, and batch verification helps only when responses arrive together (Q3). Fifth, if untrusted parties can obtain releases, the dispute path must bind each release to its record (Proposition~\ref{prop:malleable}, Lemma~\ref{lem:pacplus}).

Invalid proofs and equivocation are transferable evidence, whereas attributing non-response depends on timing\cite{lewis2025accountable}, so slashing should rest on transferable evidence. The audit cannot detect selective withholding, because canaries are unrelated to records by design (Lemma~\ref{lem:sim}); making them indistinguishable from record components would stop observers from checking that an audit opened no record (Lemma~\ref{lem:subst}), so resistance needs another mechanism, such as unpredictable dispute routing or economic commitments enforced by the deadline transcript.

% =====================================================================
\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Optimistic and verifiable computation.} Optimistic rollups rely on an honest challenger to force correct results on chain\cite{kalodner2018arbitrum}; opML applies this to machine-learning inference\cite{conway2024opml}, and EigenAI re-executes private inference in a trusted environment after a threshold key release\cite{eigenai2026}. These systems assume the challenger can read the disputed inputs; with encrypted inputs this becomes the requirement that keys be serviceable before the deadline, which KEYSTONE audits without changing the dispute game.

\paragraph{Threshold decryption and key management.} Threshold cryptosystems\cite{desmedt1990threshold}, their chosen-ciphertext-secure variants\cite{shoup2002securing} and DLEQ proofs\cite{chaum1992dleq,fiat1987prove} provide the release mechanism. Verifiable and publicly verifiable secret sharing and distributed key generation\cite{feldman1987vss,schoenmakers1999pvss,gennaro2007dkg,das2022adkg} make shares consistent when created, and proactive and dynamic sharing refreshes them\cite{herzberg1995proactive,yurek2023dpss,maram2019churp}; a refresh also exercises every share, but it is infrequent and costly. A canary response is structurally a threshold-coin share\cite{cachin2005constantinople} or a threshold-signature share on a hashed message\cite{boldyreva2003threshold}; our contribution is its use as a sampled readiness test and what that test can and cannot certify. Context-dependent threshold decryption isolates shares across contexts\cite{boneh2025context}.

\paragraph{Threshold release on ledgers.} CALYPSO releases on-ledger secrets to authorized readers through a threshold committee with an auditable access log\cite{kokoriskogias2020calypso}, and ETHTID provides threshold disclosure on Ethereum\cite{stengele2021ethtid}. Encrypted mempools face the same concerns of committees, epochs, collusion and timely decryption\cite{bebel2022ferveo,bormet2025epochless,choudhuri2024mempool}. FairBlock has a committee exchange a fixed number of identity-based decryption shares per block\cite{momeni2023fairblock}, and F3B, building on CALYPSO, has a committee release a per-transaction key once the transaction is final\cite{zhang2023f3b}. In both, timely decryption depends on a threshold of members serving the release, the property DKA makes explicit; the descriptions we found specify the release path but no pre-release readiness audit. UQ-Vote evaluates liveness of consensus-authorized threshold decryption under faults\cite{liu2026uqvote}. These ideas are established; KEYSTONE adds the deadline-bound property that release must satisfy for disputes, an audit that measures it without opening records, and an analysis of what passing it implies.

\paragraph{Proofs of storage, custody and heartbeats.} Proofs of retrievability and provable data possession spot-check stored files and bound the probability that a server missing data passes\cite{juels2007por,ateniese2007pdp}, also under a mobile adversary\cite{bowers2009hail}. KEYSTONE's audit belongs to this family, with a proof of knowledge (Lemma~\ref{lem:correct}) and sampling bounds (Theorem~\ref{thm:fa}). It differs in that possession is not service (Observation~\ref{prop:nonimpl}), in that confidentiality forces canary responses to be useless for decrypting records (Lemmas~\ref{lem:sim} and~\ref{lem:subst}), and in that DKA is a threshold, target-specific and deadline-bound property. Proof-of-custody proposals penalize validators that do not hold attested data\cite{feist2021custody}. The closest deployed analogue is the tBTC v2 heartbeat, in which each threshold wallet's signing group signs periodic messages and funds leave a wallet that fails one\cite{tbtc2026heartbeat}; KEYSTONE instead samples custodians with exact operating characteristics, audits decryption shares under a confidentiality constraint, and models readiness over time. Data-availability proofs and sampling\cite{albassam2021fraud,hallandersen2025das} concern public data, which KEYSTONE takes as given. Supplementary Table~S3 compares these mechanisms.

\paragraph{Accountability.} Slashing conditions\cite{buterin2017casper} and BFT forensics\cite{sheng2021forensics} attribute safety violations with transferable evidence, threshold traitor tracing addresses coalitions that leak decryption capability\cite{boneh2023accountability}, and attributing liveness failures depends on timing\cite{lewis2025accountable}.

% =====================================================================
\section{Threats to validity and limitations}\label{sec:validity}

\paragraph{Novelty.} The components are not new; our claim covers the property decomposition, the confidentiality-preserving audit and its analysis, and the labeled evaluation, and it rests on a bounded literature search.

\paragraph{Internal validity.} Both designs were hashed before execution, but the hashes are self-recorded and no independent party reviewed the designs; the acceptance-rule and operating-characteristic analyses were added afterwards. R2 and R2b logged thirteen deviations, among them a deadline correction before any testbed run and a restart after the host ran out of ephemeral ports; none changed an endpoint or an analysis in response to outcomes, and the corrected deadline was tested only on fresh R2b traces. 

\paragraph{Construct and external validity.} The audit measures present sampled serviceability, not future cooperation. The temporal model assumes independent exponential failures and repairs with synthetic rates, failure models are synthetic, the testbed uses loopback TCP with synthetic delays, and geo-distributed effects, ledger delay and clock skew are not measured.

\paragraph{Prototype scope.} A dealer replaces distributed key generation; the contract trusts an administrator for sampling, invalid-response evidence and cancellation; neither code nor contract has been externally audited; the lemmas hold in the random-oracle model with static corruption; and Lemma~\ref{lem:pacplus} and the temporal results are given with proof sketches here and full proofs in the supplementary material.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion and future directions}\label{sec:conclusion}

Ciphertext availability does not ensure that the threshold service needed for an encrypted-rollup dispute answers in time. We defined dispute-key availability and the weaker properties it is confused with, showed that a beacon-derived canary audit exercises real shares while its transcripts are simulatable from public data, gave its exact operating characteristics, sample sizes and sequential tests that certify a safety margin, a placement condition and a deadline budget, and showed that confidentiality against parties who obtain other releases requires binding releases to records, as record-labeled TDH2 does. For custodians that fail and recover, an exact recursion gives the risk that a dispute fails after any audit history, and a floor shows when auditing more often cannot help. The evaluation confirmed each separation: a small strict audit barely distinguishes a failed committee from a live one and alarms often on healthy committees, selective withholders pass every audit and defeat every dispute, correlated domain failures dominate risk over time, and with elliptic-curve verification off the network loop the network governs dispute completion; an order-statistic deadline held in a pre-registered replication except without network delay, where host drift of a few percent defeats any deadline without slack. Future work should address selective withholding, which the audit provably cannot detect alone; readiness models calibrated on operational data; and a production instantiation with distributed key generation and realistic ledger delays, evaluated across regions.
